tracks.title: The web, from inside a sandbox
tracks.text: Lesson zero two point thirteen — browsing. This one lives under the Nexus. The web, from inside a sandbox. Here's the shape of it. Sooner or later your software needs the web — an agent has to research, an app has to fetch a page, a job has to crawl a docs site. And browse is the runtime's answer. Three verbs — fetch one page… crawl a set or a site… search the open web — all done by the engine, on the workload's behalf… and handed back as structured data. [curious] No socket. No key. No curl. The free native browser is the default… and the provider for each verb is just a config value.

tracks.title: The three bad answers
tracks.text: First — why does this even need a lesson? Because every familiar way to give software the web is a bad one… and the parent lesson said why. You could give the workload raw network. But the workload is often a model… and anyone whose text reaches a model is partially steering it. [sighs] A prompt-injected agent with open egress is an exfiltration machine — it reads a hostile page, and POSTs your secrets somewhere on the same breath. Option two — shell out to curl. Except this runtime deliberately has no native exec. There is no shell to reach. Option three — hard-wire a paid scraping API into every caller. A key in every script… a vendor in every line… a credential one prompt-injection away from a stranger. Three bad answers… one shared mistake. They all put the web inside the workload. This lesson puts it one layer down — in the engine, where the workload can ask for the web… without ever holding it.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. Browse is the runtime's web capability. Three verbs… fulfilled by the engine on the workload's behalf… returned as structured data. With a free native browser as the default… and the provider for each verb a config value. One sentence per verb. First — fetch takes a URL, and gives back a parsed page. Second — crawl takes a list of URLs, or a single seed, and gives back many pages… concurrently, breadth-first, same host. Third — search takes a query, and gives back results. The workload never opens a socket for any of them. And browse is a general primitive… not a feature of one app. Brandnana's harvest is simply one of its callers.

tracks.title: One slot, three verbs
tracks.text: Now — one slot, three verbs. Browse is a dispatcher, and each verb picks its own provider, the moment it's called. Picture the decision as a flowchart falling top to bottom. A call comes in. First question — is this a search, and did you name a dedicated search provider? If yes… that wins outright, and we're done. If no, we ask the one question that really matters — does the configured provider declare this verb? A provider advertises what it can do through a capabilities function. So if it declares the verb… it runs. And if it doesn't… the call falls through to the free native browser, which declares all three. The native browser is the floor that nothing falls below. And one more thing, on every path — the proxy gets merged in… unless the caller already set one. Choosing a provider, and choosing a proxy… are two separate knobs that don't interfere.

tracks.title: The free browser
tracks.text: The free browser. The default provider is called Native — free, in-engine, no keys, no external service. It's pure BEAM. Erlang's own SSL and HTTP doing the fetching… a lightweight extractor turning HTML into structure… and a concurrent crawler. Three small bricks — let me name each one and its real defaults. First brick… Fetch — a pure-Erlang GET, no Rust, no port, no sidecar, following redirects by hand. Its defaults — a twenty-second timeout, and five redirects maximum. Second brick… Extract — zero-dependency regex and tag-strip, pulling out the title, the meta tags, the headings, the links, and the readable text. Its defaults — headings capped at sixty… text capped at four thousand characters. Third brick… Crawl — fan-out over a URL list, or breadth-first from one seed. Its defaults — eight requests wide… twenty-five pages… depth two. And the through-line of all three… every default is conservative on purpose, and no part of this asks for a credential — because no part talks to anyone but the origin server.

tracks.title: Dressing like a browser
tracks.text: Here's the part that surprises people — dressing like a browser. A bare HTTP client looks nothing like a browser, and many sites notice. So Fetch shapes its TLS handshake to resemble one — and it does it from pure Elixir, with no native dependency. [curious] There are named profiles — default, chrome, and safari — and the default is chrome. The chrome and safari profiles force the version posture a real browser ships with — TLS one-point-three, then one-point-two. They reorder the cipher list. And they set the elliptic curves a browser offers — x-two-five-five-one-nine first. On top of that ride real browser headers — a genuine Chrome one-twenty-four user-agent, with matching accept lines. Now hold the two profiles side by side. The default profile takes the library's posture as given. The chrome profile overrides all of it — forced versions, reordered ciphers, browser curves, a real Chrome string. The verdict — the chrome profile is the one that dresses for the part. And a spike proved the point that matters — the same endpoint completes under default TLS one-three… and under forced TLS one-two with reordered ciphers. The handshake is ours to shape, from the BEAM. The honest limit — stated right in the code — is that these profiles approximate a browser's posture. A byte-exact fingerprint, the kind that produces a matching hash… is future work. Real control today… pixel-for-pixel mimicry not yet.

tracks.title: Pages come back as org
tracks.text: Pages come back as org — and this is the signature move. Extract does not return raw HTML, or some bespoke blob you have to learn. A fetched page is a small, stable shape — url, title, description, headings, links, and readable text. And from that shape, it renders org… the same grammar everything else in the system already speaks. So a browse result drops straight into the workbook's context repository. Let me read you the real node a fetch produces. A top headline — Elixir version one-sixteen, Documentation — tagged source, point. Then a properties drawer — the URL is hexdocs dot p-m slash elixir… the host is hexdocs dot p-m. Then a sub-heading called outline — getting started… modules and functions. Then a sub-heading called links — one entry, pointing at the Kernel page. And finally a sub-heading called text — the readable body, beginning… Elixir is a dynamic, functional language for building scalable. [excited] A web page… landed as the same org the rest of the system reads and writes. Links capped at forty, text at four thousand characters, by design — so a single fetch can't flood the context with a whole site. A crawl concatenates its pages into one org document, headed… browse crawl, N pages. The web stops being a foreign format the moment it crosses the engine boundary.

tracks.title: BFS on the BEAM
tracks.text: Breadth-first search, on the BEAM. Crawl has two entry points. The first takes a known list of URLs and fetches them concurrently. The second takes a single seed, and walks breadth-first — following only same-host links, defaulting to twenty-five pages at depth two. Both fan out eight requests wide… no thread pool, no sidecar… with a twenty-five second per-task timeout. Picture the loop as a story. A seed becomes the frontier — the URLs not yet visited. The frontier fans out, eight at a time. Whatever comes back has its same-host links harvested, and fed into the next wave. And whatever does not come back… is simply dropped. [curious] A dead URL doesn't sink the crawl — the result is everything that returned, not a demand that everything return. The loop exits when it hits the page cap or the depth limit… and hands back the pages it gathered. This is the BEAM's millions-of-cheap-processes claim… doing ordinary work.

tracks.title: Search and the datacenter wall
tracks.text: Search… and the datacenter wall. This carries the truest war story in the whole codebase. Native search scrapes the result pages of real engines — DuckDuckGo, Brave, and Bing — trying DuckDuckGo's HTML endpoint first because it's the most scrape-stable, and taking the first engine that returns anything. And it works beautifully… on a laptop. Here's the picture as a fork in the road. The query arrives, and asks one question — is there a real search API key set? On a laptop, you don't bother — the residential IP sails straight through the scrape engines, and you never think about it. But on a cloud box… [sighs] those keyless scrape engines return empty. Because non-residential traffic gets served captchas instead of results. So web search silently finds nothing — and this stranded the project's own landing site, even with a strong model behind it. That's the cloud answer. When the DataForSEO key is set, browse goes through a real SERP API first — a US-located Google query — and only falls through to scraping if that's absent or errors. So the fork is the whole story. Laptop — scrape, and it just works. Cloud — the captcha wall, and you need the API lane. One environment variable… moves the laptop answer to the cloud answer.

tracks.title: Swapping the engine of the engine
tracks.text: Swapping the engine of the engine. Native can't run JavaScript, or beat a bot-wall — and that's exactly why the provider slot exists. The shipped, proven example is Firecrawl. It renders JavaScript, defeats bot-walls, and it slots in with one config line — set the browse provider to Firecrawl. That's the entire change. Every fetch, crawl, and search now routes to Firecrawl instead of Native — and no caller changes. Not even brandnana's harvest. Picture the exchange as a conversation. A caller asks Browse to fetch a URL. Browse asks Firecrawl, which renders the page with a real browser engine — JavaScript executed, bot-wall passed — and hands back the finished HTML. Browse runs that HTML through the very same extractor the native browser uses. And the caller gets back… the same page shape it always gets. [curious] The caller cannot tell which provider ran. That's the contract — every provider converges on one output type. Two more facts complete the slot. First — every provider method is an optional callback, so a partial provider implements only what it can do, and its capabilities function declares exactly that. Second — the proxy is its own knob. A host-port pair, or a zero-arity function that returns one… and a rotating-proxy service turns the vanilla browser into a fuller scraper. A real Firecrawl key shipped as a fly secret — proving the slot, in production.

tracks.title: Who gets to browse
tracks.text: Who gets to browse. Browse is a capability with three consumer surfaces… and a policy that decides who reaches it. Let me walk the three doors, because they all return the same structured page. First door — agent tools. An agent calls web search or fetch, and gets back a clean bulleted list — title, url, snippet. This is the research capability the agents regained when the old run-and-curl hatch was removed. Second door — the Dock import, called browse-fetch. A WASM component imports it, and the host owns network egress, so the component never opens a socket — no raw HTTP, no sockets granted. It just receives a JSON page string. Third door — a POST to slash api slash browse, on the authed control plane — returning org, or JSON, depending on the request. Same capability… three doors… one shape coming back. And the gate is by construction, not by checkbox. Browse is granted by the network and posix profiles — and denied by minimal and compute. [excited] A component that hard-imports browse-fetch under minimal doesn't get a polite runtime error… it fails to link. The denial is in the wiring — proven end to end by a real test that watches the unprivileged build refuse to come together.

tracks.title: What the free browser isn't
tracks.text: Now the honest part — what the free browser isn't. And every limit here has its escape hatch built into the same design. First — no JavaScript, no bot-wall victories. The hatch — one config line swaps in Firecrawl. Second — the TLS fingerprint approximates; byte-exact is future work. The hatch — the proxy knob, and an external provider. Third — Extract is regex-grade; no CSS selectors or table parsing yet. The hatch — Floki is the stated upgrade, and the page contract won't move when it lands. Fourth — keyless search dies on datacenter IPs. The hatch — one environment variable, or a configured search provider. Fifth — proxied fetches serialize, because the HTTP proxy setting is process-global. The hatch — a per-proxy connection pool is a stated follow-up, and unproxied fetches stay concurrent. And sixth — one proven external provider ships, Firecrawl; an Exa module does not exist yet. The hatch — the slot is the same regardless. Anything that returns the page shape… drops in. [curious] Notice the pattern — each limit names its own door out. That's not a coincidence. That's the design.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Is it really free out of the box? Yes — pure BEAM, no keys, no meter. Your agent can fetch, crawl, and search the minute the engine is up… and what comes back is structured. Why is search empty on my cloud deploy? Because keyless scraping returns nothing from datacenter IPs — the captcha wall. The fix is one secret — set the DataForSEO auth, and search goes API-first. Do my agents hold the Firecrawl key? No. The key lives in the engine's environment, and never enters the sandbox. A prompt-injected agent can't leak a key it was never handed. Can a workbook just open a socket instead? Only with the network capability — and even then, browse is the brokered lane that exists so it usually doesn't have to. And — does it respect robots dot text? Honestly… no. There's no robots handling in the code today. Crawl limits itself to same-host links under a page cap, but that's politeness by accident, not by policy. [sighs] If you need robots compliance, that's a gap to close — and we'd rather say so than imply a check that isn't there.

tracks.title: Back up to the Nexus
tracks.text: So that's browsing. The web, from inside a sandbox — fetched by the engine, handed back as structured data… as org. No socket… no key… no curl, ever, inside the workload. The free native browser is the default… and the provider is a config value you can change in one line, while every caller keeps working. [curious] This was the capability and grant model… applied to the web. So the way back up is short — the Nexus, the parent lesson, holds the rest of that doctrine. The capabilities. The grants. And the exfiltration framing that made all three bad answers… bad. Go read it next.
